definition: A reaction that gives out heat energy to the surroundings. Products have less chemical energy than reactants; the temperature of the mixture and its surroundings rises; ∆H is negative.
msAccepts: gives out heat to the surroundings
temperature of the surroundings increases
products have less energy than reactants
msAvoids: saying heat is destroyed
confusing 'gives out heat' with 'needs a flame'
omitting the surroundings from the heat-flow direction

definition: A reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings. Products have more chemical energy than reactants; the temperature of the mixture and its surroundings falls; ∆H is positive.
msAccepts: takes in heat from the surroundings
temperature of the surroundings decreases
products have more energy than reactants
msAvoids: claiming every heated reaction is endothermic
saying cold is added
omitting the surroundings from the heat-flow direction

definition: The heat energy taken in or given out during a chemical reaction — the difference between the energy of the products and the reactants. Only the change (∆H) is measurable, never absolute enthalpy.
msAccepts: heat energy change of a reaction at constant pressure
difference in energy between products and reactants
∆H
msAvoids: calling it the total energy a substance contains
quoting ∆H without a sign
units in J instead of kJ/mol

definition: Describes the relative energies of reactants and products: the more energy a chemical has, the less stable it is. Exothermic products are more stable than the reactants that formed them.
msAccepts: more energy means less stable
products lower in energy are more stable
msAvoids: equating stability with inertness
saying unstable substances always decompose

definition: The unit for the amount of a substance. Molar enthalpy changes and bond energies are both quoted per mole, so mole arithmetic from u1:c05 feeds every calculation in this chapter.
msAccepts: unit for amount of substance
6.02 × 10²³ particles
mass ÷ relative formula mass
msAvoids: confusing the mole with molarity
quoting ∆H per gram instead of per mole

definition: A chart with energy on the vertical axis and progress of the reaction on the horizontal axis. Reactants and products sit on levels; the arrow and ∆H sign show the direction of the energy change.
msAccepts: energy axis labelled
reactant and product levels
arrow up for endothermic, down for exothermic
msAvoids: drawing an unlabelled energy axis
putting exothermic products above the reactants
omitting the ∆H sign beside the arrow

definition: Breaking a compound down by heating — an endothermic change that needs the heat supplied continuously. Metal carbonates decompose to the metal oxide and carbon dioxide on heating.
msAccepts: decomposition caused by heat
endothermic because heating continues throughout
msAvoids: listing it as exothermic because a flame is present
omitting the products' identity

definition: The heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 gram of a substance by 1 °C. Water's value is 4.18 J/g/°C; the same quantity governs cooling in the reverse direction.
msAccepts: energy to raise 1 g by 1 °C
4.18 J/g/°C for water
J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹
msAvoids: using the mass of fuel instead of water in Q = mc∆T
claiming it applies only to heating

definition: The container a calorimetry experiment runs in — a copper can in the combustion experiment, a polystyrene cup for reactions in solution. Its contents are the known mass that absorbs or releases the heat.
msAccepts: vessel holding the substance heated
copper can or polystyrene cup examples
msAvoids: calling the spirit burner the calorimeter
ignoring that the can itself warms up (an error source)

definition: Measuring heat changes by letting a reaction warm or cool a known mass of water, then calculating with Q = mc∆T and dividing by moles for the molar enthalpy change.
msAccepts: experiment measuring temperature change of water
Q = mc∆T applied to a reaction mixture
msAvoids: describing it without the water-mass step
forgetting the assumptions (density and shc of water)

definition: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of a substance is burned completely. Always negative for burning; measured for alcohols with the spirit-burner-and-copper-can experiment.
msAccepts: ∆H when 1 mol burns
negative sign with rising temperature evidence
msAvoids: quoting the heat released in the experiment as the answer
omitting 'per mole'

definition: The heat energy change divided by the number of moles of reactant consumed (∆H = Q ÷ n), in kJ/mol. The moles used must be the limiting reactant's, and the sign follows the temperature trend.
msAccepts: Q ÷ n with n in moles
kJ/mol units
sign matching exothermic or endothermic direction
msAvoids: dividing by the excess reactant's moles
leaving the answer in J
dropping the sign

definition: Burning with insufficient oxygen; releases less heat than complete combustion and produces carbon (soot) instead of only carbon dioxide. Seen as a yellow-orange rather than blue flame.
msAccepts: less oxygen than needed
less energy released than complete combustion
soot/carbon evidence
msAvoids: saying no combustion happens
missing the observation-based evidence

definition: A reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive one in a compound (a competition reaction). Zinc displacing copper from copper(II) sulfate is the calorimetry example here.
msAccepts: more reactive element displaces a less reactive one
competition reaction
msAvoids: calling precipitation a displacement
forgetting the ionic bookkeeping in the equation

definition: More than enough of a reactant to ensure the other reactant is fully used up. The excess reactant's moles never enter ∆H = Q ÷ n — the limiting reactant's do.
msAccepts: more than enough to react everything else
limiting reactant determines the moles in ∆H = Q/n
msAvoids: dividing Q by the excess moles
confusing excess with leftover being wasted entirely

definition: A physical process in which a salt's particles separate into water. Depending on the salt it releases heat (exothermic) or absorbs heat (endothermic) — the thermometer decides.
msAccepts: physical process, not a chemical reaction
can be exothermic or endothermic depending on the salt
msAvoids: calling dissolving a chemical reaction
assuming all dissolvings cool

definition: The reaction between an alkali and an acid — essentially OH⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) → H₂O(l). Exothermic; measured here with the two-best-fit-lines graph that also yields an unknown acid concentration.
msAccepts: acid + alkali forms salt and water
H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O ionic equation
exothermic temperature rise
msAvoids: saying the ionic equation needs spectator ions
omitting state symbols in the ionic equation

definition: The small amount of energy needed to get a reaction started — beginning the bond-breaking in the reactants. Even strongly exothermic reactions need it; a flame is often its source.
msAccepts: minimum energy to start a reaction
needed to begin breaking reactant bonds
msAvoids: confusing it with the overall ∆H
saying it changes the final ∆H value

definition: The energy needed to break 1 mole of covalent bonds in gaseous molecules, in kJ/mol; the same quantity is released when the bonds form. Quoted values are averages for estimates.
msAccepts: energy to break 1 mol of specified bonds in the gas state
same value released on bond formation
kJ/mol
msAvoids: per-molecule interpretation
applying to ionic compounds
treating averages as exact values

definition: Calcium oxide, CaO. Adding water slakes it — a strongly exothermic reaction producing steam — and the calcium hydroxide formed is called slaked lime.
msAccepts: calcium oxide
slaking gives calcium hydroxide (slaked lime)
msAvoids: confusing quicklime with limestone (calcium carbonate)
missing the exothermic character of slaking

definition: The overall heat released or absorbed by a reaction is the same however the reaction is carried out, provided reactants and products are identical — even if the calculated route is imaginary.
msAccepts: enthalpy change is route-independent
same reactants and products give the same ∆H
msAvoids: claiming real reactions proceed via the imagined bond-breaking route
quoting it without the condition

definition: A measure of the number of ways the energy in a system can be distributed; greater in more disordered systems. Solids have lower entropy than liquids, liquids lower than gases.
msAccepts: measure of disorder / ways of distributing energy
solid < liquid < gas ordering
entropy increase drives otherwise unfavourable changes
msAvoids: defining it as 'randomness' with no energy context
requiring entropy calculations at this level
